Compiler note: Both options marked with question marks; no answer endorsed.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A child presents with vomiting and diarrhea about seven times a day, very dry skin and mucous membranes, sunken eyes, delayed capillary refill 4 seconds, lethargy, and blood pressure 75/43 mmHg. What type of dehydration does this child have?
why_right: The child has severe dehydration signs (very dry mucosa, sunken eyes, "lethargy") plus signs of circulatory failure: capillary refill "4 seconds" and hypotension "75/43 mmHg". Dehydration with hypotension and poor perfusion is decompensated hypovolemic shock, which needs an immediate 20 mL/kg isotonic bolus.
why_wrong_block:
A. Mild dehydration: child is alert and thirsty with normal eyes, wet tongue, normal pulse and normal capillary refill; this child is lethargic and hypotensive.
B. Moderate dehydration: irritable, sunken eyes, dry tongue, slow skin pinch, but still alert with maintained blood pressure; lethargy plus hypotension takes this beyond moderate.
D. No dehydration: no signs at all; this child has seven episodes a day of losses with clear clinical dehydration.
key_concept:
Grade dehydration by mental state and circulation.
  • Mild: alert, thirsty, normal exam, weight loss below 5%
  • Moderate: irritable, sunken eyes, dry tongue, slow skin pinch, 6 to 9%
  • Severe: drowsy or unconscious, very slow skin pinch, weak thready pulse, 10% or more
  • Shock: prolonged capillary refill, cold extremities, hypotension (late sign in children)
  • Treatment of shock: 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus, reassess, repeat
exam_pearl: Hypotension is a LATE sign in children; once present with dehydration signs, call it shock, not just moderate dehydration.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Restated on next page as 'Q:' (with 'hypotension' instead of BP value), Answer: C. Hypovolemic shock.

stem: A newborn presented with bleeding from the umbilical stump. Labs showed prolonged PT and aPTT and normal platelet count. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A newborn bleeding from the "umbilical stump" with "prolonged PT and aPTT" and a "normal platelet count" is hemorrhagic disease of the newborn. Vitamin K is needed for factors II, VII, IX and X, so both the extrinsic (PT, factor VII) and intrinsic (aPTT, factor IX) pathways are affected; newborns have low stores, especially without prophylaxis at birth. Treatment is parenteral vitamin K1.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hemophilia A (factor VIII) prolongs the aPTT only with a normal PT; it presents with hemarthrosis or circumcision bleeding, not a prolonged PT.
B. Von Willebrand disease gives mucosal bleeding (epistaxis, gums, menorrhagia, dental extraction) with prolonged bleeding time and normal or mildly prolonged aPTT; the PT stays normal.
key_concept:
Read the coag pattern first.
  • PT and aPTT both prolonged, normal platelets: vitamin K deficiency (or liver disease, DIC with low platelets)
  • Isolated aPTT prolonged: hemophilia A or B
  • Prolonged bleeding time, normal PT: vWD or platelet disorder
  • Umbilical bleeding with normal PT and aPTT: think factor XIII deficiency
  • Risks for neonatal vitamin K deficiency: home birth, no prophylaxis, exclusive breastfeeding, maternal anticonvulsants
exam_pearl: Delayed cord SEPARATION with infections (normal coags) is leukocyte adhesion deficiency; cord BLEEDING with prolonged PT and aPTT is vitamin K deficiency.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed recall: 'Baby delayed separation of umbilical cords and bleeding from umbilical stump. Labs of coagulation' with options hemophilia A / Von Willebrand disease / vit K deficiency / Thrombocytopenia (unmarked).

stem: pt after MVC come with low bp and maybe tachycardia what is initial step
OptA: iv fluid intervention (like this i dont remember)
key_concept:
Trauma + hypotension = hemorrhage until proven otherwise; restore volume and control bleeding before any vasopressor.
  • Hypovolemic (tachycardia, cold peripheries): IV access, fluid/blood, find and stop the bleed
  • Neurogenic (bradycardia, warm, spinal injury): fluids first, then vasopressor
  • Obstructive (distended neck veins): tamponade or tension pneumothorax, decompress
  • Vasopressors only after adequate volume, in distributive shock
exam_pearl: Tachycardia points to blood loss and volume first; hypotension with bradycardia after spinal injury is the scenario where a vasopressor enters early.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A Child is 24 months, doesn’t respond to his name does not talk yet, no eye contact, plays alone. Mother noticed he arranges toys in a straight line
highlight_terms_source: arranges toys in a straight line
why_right: At "24 months" the child has the social communication triad of autism: no response to name, "no eye contact", "plays alone", plus restricted repetitive behavior ("arranges toys in a straight line"). Lining up toys and absent joint attention are not explained by deafness or an isolated speech delay, so the next step is formal autism screening (for example M-CHAT, recommended at 18 and 24 months) and referral for diagnostic evaluation.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hearing test is right for an isolated speech or language delay with otherwise normal social interaction; it is part of the autism work-up, but it does not explain absent eye contact and repetitive toy lining.
C. Speech therapy referral treats a pure expressive language delay; here the core problem is social communication and repetitive behavior, which needs autism assessment first.
key_concept:
Speech delay plus social and repetitive features = screen for autism.
  • Social: poor eye contact, no response to name, no pointing or shared attention, plays alone
  • Restricted or repetitive: lining up toys, hand flapping, insistence on sameness
  • Routine ASD screening at 18 and 24 months
  • Isolated speech delay with normal social skills: hearing test first
  • Loss of previously acquired words or social skills at any age is a red flag
exam_pearl: Pure speech delay points to the ears; speech delay plus no eye contact and lined-up toys points to autism.

stem: A 2 month old his mother mentioned noticed his right eye goes inward while feeding, she's concerned, what's the most initial management? I Am Not Sure If Same Recall Or Not, But It Had Normal Red Reflex & Corneal Reflex
why_right: A 2 month old whose eye goes inward while feeding (intermittent) with a normal red reflex and normal corneal light reflex has no sign of true strabismus or intraocular pathology. Intermittent misalignment is normal at this age, so the initial management is to reassure and recheck.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT is not used to assess infant ocular alignment; imaging is reserved for abnormal findings such as leukocoria, proptosis or neurological signs.
B. Ophthalmology referral is right for a constant deviation at any age, a deviation persisting beyond about 4 to 6 months, an abnormal red reflex or an asymmetric corneal light reflex.
key_concept:
Infant eye alignment: intermittent misalignment in the first months is normal; constant or persistent deviation is not.
  • Under about 4 months, intermittent, normal red reflex: reassure and recheck
  • Constant deviation at any age: refer
  • Any deviation persisting after about 4 to 6 months: refer (amblyopia risk)
  • Abnormal or absent red reflex: urgent referral (retinoblastoma, cataract)
  • Symmetric corneal light reflex with apparent squint: pseudostrabismus (epicanthal folds)
exam_pearl: An abnormal red reflex flips this to urgent ophthalmology referral; an asymmetric corneal light reflex or constant deviation also needs referral.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0331).

stem: A 6 month old pediatric came with convergence and esotropia and during exam Intact corneal light reflex The parents are concerned what should you do?
why_right: The decisive clue is an intact (symmetric) corneal light reflex. The Hirschberg test is the screening test for strabismus: if the reflexes are centred and symmetric the eyes are truly aligned, and the apparent inward turning is pseudoesotropia, usually from a broad nasal bridge and epicanthal folds. The parents should be reassured.
why_wrong_block: B. Referral is right when the corneal light reflex is displaced (temporally in the deviated eye in esotropia), the cover test shows movement, the deviation is constant, or the red reflex is abnormal.
key_concept:
Apparent squint + symmetric corneal light reflex = pseudostrabismus: reassure.
  • Hirschberg: reflex centred and symmetric = aligned
  • Esotropia: reflex displaced temporally in the deviated eye
  • Exotropia: reflex displaced nasally
  • True strabismus persisting beyond about 4 to 6 months: refer (amblyopia)
exam_pearl: The parents' concern does not change management; the corneal light reflex does. Asymmetric reflex = refer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Infant <6 months with intermittent esotropia + normal corneal reflex: normal, reassure. Persistent/constant deviation after 6 months: refer.

stem: 26 years old primigravida presented 10 days after vaginal delivery complaining of fever and back pain. On examination, lower back tenderness lower limb weakness, and incontinence. Diagnosis of spinal epidural abscess was made. Most appropriate management?
why_right: Spinal epidural abscess with an established neurological deficit (lower limb weakness and incontinence) is a surgical emergency: urgent surgical decompression and drainage, combined with IV antibiotics, gives the best chance of neurological recovery. The recent obstetric epidural is the likely route of infection, and fever with focal back tenderness completes the classic picture.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antibiotics are always given, but antibiotics alone are reserved for patients with no neurological deficit or who are unfit for surgery; with weakness and sphincter loss, delaying decompression risks permanent paralysis.
C. Image-guided needle aspiration is an option only in selected patients without deficit (or poor surgical candidates); it cannot decompress a cord or cauda equina already compromised.
D. Observation wastes the time window; any new or progressing deficit in epidural abscess needs urgent decompression.
key_concept:
Spinal epidural abscess: fever + focal back pain/tenderness + neurological deficit; MRI with contrast confirms.
  • Risk: recent epidural/spinal procedure, IV drug use, diabetes, bacteremia
  • Commonest organism: Staphylococcus aureus
  • Neurological deficit present: urgent surgical decompression + IV antibiotics
  • No deficit or unfit for surgery: IV antibiotics ± image-guided aspiration with close neuro monitoring
exam_pearl: The moment weakness or bladder/bowel dysfunction appears, the answer moves from antibiotics to surgery.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed recall: 'Patient delivered with epidural anesthesia, after 1 week she presented to ED with low back pain with lower paresis and bowel dysfunction, it was abscess. What to do?' A. Surgical drainage (highlighted) B. Needle aspiration.

stem: A 4-year-old girl was bitten by a newly adopted cat. The cat is febrile and lethargic. There is no redness at the bite site. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: The biting cat is "newly adopted" (unknown vaccination history) and is "febrile and lethargic", so it must be treated as possibly rabid. A bite that breaks the skin is a high-risk (category III) exposure, and an unvaccinated child needs rabies immunoglobulin into and around the wound plus a full rabies vaccine course, started immediately without waiting for the animal's outcome.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassure is only acceptable for a healthy, vaccinated animal that can be observed for 10 days, or for exposures with no broken skin; a sick animal makes this a rabies risk.
B. Prophylactic antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate) are considered for cat bites because of Pasteurella, especially punctures or hand wounds, but they do nothing for the life-threatening rabies risk and the wound shows no infection.
C. Irrigation with soap and water is always done for every bite, but irrigation ONLY leaves the child without rabies post-exposure prophylaxis despite a suspicious animal.
key_concept:
Animal bite decision: is the animal possibly rabid?
  • Always: wash and irrigate the wound thoroughly, tetanus status
  • Healthy domestic dog or cat available: observe animal 10 days, start PEP if it becomes ill
  • Sick, rabid-looking, or unavailable animal: start PEP now
  • Unvaccinated person, category III (broken skin): rabies immunoglobulin plus vaccine
  • Previously vaccinated person: vaccine boosters only, no immunoglobulin
exam_pearl: "Febrile and lethargic" animal is the clue that turns a simple bite into rabies PEP with BOTH immunoglobulin and vaccine.

stem: A 4-year-old girl was bitten by a newly adopted cat. The cat is febrile and lethargic. There is no redness at the bite site. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: no redness at the bite site
why_right: The cat is "newly adopted" with unknown vaccination and is "febrile and lethargic", so rabies must be presumed. A bite with broken skin in a previously unvaccinated child needs full post-exposure prophylaxis: rabies immunoglobulin for immediate passive antibodies (infiltrated around the wound) plus the vaccine course for active long-term immunity.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance fits a healthy, observable, vaccinated pet or contact without broken skin; a sick animal makes it unsafe.
B. Vaccine alone is right for minor (category II) exposures such as nibbling or minor scratches without bleeding, or for a previously vaccinated person; a bite needs immunoglobulin as well, because vaccine antibodies take about a week to appear.
C. Immunoglobulin alone gives only short-lived passive protection; it is never given without the vaccine series.
key_concept:
Rabies PEP by exposure category (unvaccinated person).
  • Category I (touching, licks on intact skin): no PEP
  • Category II (nibbling, minor scratch without bleeding): wound care plus vaccine
  • Category III (bite or scratch breaking skin, licks on broken skin or mucosa): wound care plus immunoglobulin plus vaccine
  • Previously vaccinated: vaccine boosters only
  • Wound irrigation is always the first local measure
exam_pearl: Some recall versions add "irrigate wound"; it is always done, but the management decision tested is immunoglobulin plus vaccine for a suspect animal.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Typed 418 version had options A. Reassure B. Give prophylactic antibiotics C. Irrigate wound D. Give rabies immunoglobulin and vaccine, with C. Irrigate wound highlighted. The 'Q:' version (used here) notes: '100% sure about the case and options. NO irrigate wound as a choice.'
Other marked answers: Typed 418 version: C. Irrigate wound

stem: A 42-year-old woman involved in a head on collision arrived at the Emergency Room talking coherently, with the following vital signs. Her examination revealed equal air entry bilaterally with ecchymosis on her anterior chest wall, distended neck veins and her abdomen is soft and lax. Blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, Heart rate 130/min, Respiratory rate 18/min Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: ecchymosis on her anterior chest wall
why_right: After blunt chest trauma (anterior chest wall ecchymosis), the patient has distended neck veins and hypotension (90/60) with tachycardia: two parts of Beck triad, which is enough to call cardiac tamponade. Equal air entry bilaterally with a normal respiratory rate argues against the other obstructive cause, tension pneumothorax, and the soft abdomen makes intra-abdominal bleeding less likely.
why_wrong_block:
B. Cardiac contusion usually presents with arrhythmias or ECG changes (and troponin rise); it does not explain raised neck veins with clear, equal lungs as well as tamponade does.
C. Massive hemothorax gives reduced air entry and dullness on one side, with flat neck veins from blood loss; here air entry is equal and veins are distended.
D. Tension pneumothorax gives absent breath sounds, hyperresonance and tracheal shift; a bilateral one would leave her in severe respiratory distress with silent chests, not talking comfortably with RR 18 and normal air entry on both sides.
key_concept:
Distended neck veins + hypotension after chest trauma = obstructive shock; breath sounds decide which one.
  • Equal air entry, (muffled heart sounds): cardiac tamponade, treat with pericardiocentesis / surgical drainage
  • Absent breath sounds, hyperresonant, trachea shifted: tension pneumothorax, needle decompression then chest tube
  • Dull, reduced air entry, flat neck veins: massive hemothorax, chest tube ± thoracotomy
  • Beck triad: hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds
exam_pearl: Raised JVP with equal air entry is tamponade; raised JVP with one silent hemithorax is tension pneumothorax.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Related 'Q:' version: patient stabbed in chest with hypotension, tachycardia, muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins, clear lungs; options Myocardial contusion / Hemothorax / Tension pneumothorax / Cardiac tamponade; Answer: D. Cardiac tamponade.

stem: A 2-years old child develops tonic-clonic convulsions for 3 minutes, he is drowsy but responsive. Temperature of 39, sore throat and runny nose, parents reported no past medical history, positive family history of febrile convulsions. Parents asking for consultation?
OptA: Reassurance, and find the source of fever
why_right: A "2-years old" child with a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting "3 minutes" during a fever of "39" from a viral URTI ("sore throat and runny nose"), no past history, and a positive family history is a simple febrile seizure. Postictal drowsiness with responsiveness is expected. Management is reassurance, antipyretics for comfort, and finding and treating the fever source.
why_wrong_block:
B. Prophylactic antiepileptics are not recommended for simple febrile seizures, because the prognosis is excellent and drug side effects outweigh any benefit; antiepileptics fit epilepsy (2 or more unprovoked seizures).
C. Urgent CT brain is for focal deficits, head trauma, signs of raised ICP, or persistently altered consciousness; a quick recovery after a short generalized seizure does not need imaging.
D. EEG is not needed after a simple febrile seizure; it is used for unprovoked seizures or suspected epilepsy.
key_concept:
Febrile seizure: age 6 months to 6 years with fever and no CNS infection.
  • Simple: generalized, under 15 minutes, once in 24 hours, quick recovery
  • Complex: focal, over 15 minutes, or recurs within 24 hours
  • Simple: reassure, antipyretic, treat source; no CT, EEG or AED
  • Lumbar puncture if meningeal signs or suspicion of meningitis (lower threshold in infants)
  • Seizure lasting 5 minutes or more: treat as status with a benzodiazepine
exam_pearl: Antipyretics improve comfort but do not prevent recurrence; tell parents this when reassuring.

stem: A 10 years old girl, came to the ED after transient loss of consciousness with falling while she was running. She is healthy with no chronic illnesses. Examination unremarkable except ejection systolic murmur. What should you do?
why_right: Syncope "while she was running" (exertional) is a red flag for a cardiac cause, and the "ejection systolic murmur" suggests left ventricular outflow obstruction such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or aortic stenosis. Echocardiography directly shows the structure (septal hypertrophy, valve stenosis) and is the most appropriate test; this recall's key separates the quick next step (ECG) from the most appropriate diagnostic test (echo).
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance is for typical vasovagal syncope (prodrome, upright posture, trigger) with a normal exam and ECG; exertional syncope with a murmur is never reassured.
B. Electrolytes help when vomiting, diarrhea, eating disorder or drugs suggest an arrhythmia from hypokalemia; nothing here points to that.
D. ECG is done early in every syncope and screens for long QT, WPW or LVH; it would be the answer if the question asked for the initial or next test, but it cannot define the outflow lesion causing the murmur.
key_concept:
Syncope red flags demand cardiac evaluation.
  • Red flags: during exertion, while supine, chest pain or palpitations, family history of sudden death, abnormal exam
  • Ejection systolic murmur plus exertional syncope: HCM or aortic stenosis, confirm with echo
  • HCM murmur increases with Valsalva or standing, decreases with squatting
  • Typical vasovagal with normal ECG: reassure and explain
exam_pearl: Read the lead-in: "next" or "initial" favors ECG; "most appropriate" or "diagnostic" with a murmur favors echo.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Next: D. Electrocardiogram. Most appropriate: C. Echocardiogram.

stem: A child who lives with his grandfather known to be tuberculosis (TB) positive presents with fever and weight loss. His PPD test is positive, and chest X-ray reveals right upper lobe consolidation. What is the most appropriate treatment regimen?
OptC: INH, rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide for 2 months, then INH and rifampicin for 4 months
why_right: Household contact with a TB patient, "fever and weight loss", a "positive PPD" and "right upper lobe consolidation" means active pulmonary TB, not latent infection. Active TB needs multidrug therapy: an intensive phase of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months, then a continuation phase of isoniazid and rifampicin for 4 months.
why_wrong_block:
A. Rifampicin monotherapy treats latent TB (usually for 4 months); using one drug for active disease breeds resistance.
B. Isoniazid plus rifampicin for 3 months is a latent TB regimen for a positive test with a normal chest X-ray and no symptoms; this child has symptoms and consolidation.
key_concept:
Latent vs active TB decides the regimen.
  • Latent (positive test, no symptoms, normal CXR): isoniazid 6 to 9 months, rifampicin 4 months, or isoniazid plus rifampicin 3 months
  • Active pulmonary: 2 months HRZE then 4 months HR
  • TB meningitis: longer course plus dexamethasone
  • Give pyridoxine with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy
  • Close contacts with TST 5 mm or more count as positive
exam_pearl: Symptoms plus an abnormal chest X-ray make it active TB; never treat active disease with a one or two drug latent regimen.

stem: Patient with cystic fibrosis abdominal pain after eating food with high fat and protein. What's the appropriate diet?
why_right: In cystic fibrosis, thick secretions block the pancreatic ducts causing exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, so fat and protein are not digested; pain and steatorrhea "after eating food with high fat and protein" reflect malabsorption. The fix is pancreatic enzyme replacement with every meal and snack while continuing a high-calorie, high-fat diet, plus fat-soluble vitamin supplements.
why_wrong_block:
B. No carbs eating removes a major energy source when CF patients need extra calories; carbohydrate does not cause the pain, and even CF-related diabetes is managed with insulin rather than carbohydrate restriction.
C. Multivitamins alone (fat-soluble A, D, E, K) are needed in CF, but without enzymes the fat and protein, and the vitamins themselves, are still malabsorbed.
D. Decreasing fat worsens the energy deficit; CF diets are deliberately high fat (around 35 to 40% of calories) with enzyme cover, unlike other malabsorption states.
key_concept:
CF nutrition: high calorie, high fat, with enzymes.
  • Pancreatic insufficiency: steatorrhea, foul bulky stools, failure to thrive
  • Enzymes (lipase) with every meal and snack
  • Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K
  • Extra salt in hot climates and with exercise
  • Watch for CF-related diabetes and liver disease
exam_pearl: Unlike most malabsorption, CF is NOT treated by cutting fat; replace the enzymes and keep the fat high.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Another recall ('Q:'): parents gave high protein and high fat diet for him to gain weight but without improvement; main complaint increasing foul smelling stools (steatorrhea) of CF; he was on the 20-something percentile and now deteriorating; clear chest. Options: A. start pancreatic enzymes therapy (highlighted) B. Multivitamins only C. High fiber low fats or proteins (recaller chose it) D. Low calorie diet.

stem: a 5-month-old infant presents with a 10-day history of cough and episodes of cyanosis, accompanied by post-tussive vomiting. Laboratory results show a white blood cell count of 27 with 80% lymphocytes. Which of the following is the most appropriate management
why_right: A 5-month-old with 10 days of cough, paroxysms followed by cyanosis and post-tussive vomiting is pertussis, and the WBC 27 with 80% lymphocytes (marked lymphocytosis) clinches it. Treatment and prophylaxis for close contacts is a macrolide; azithromycin is the preferred macrolide in young infants. Antibiotics shorten infectivity and are given to infants even when the paroxysmal phase has started.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ceftriaxone: covers typical bacterial pneumonia, sepsis and meningitis, but has no reliable activity against Bordetella pertussis. Right when the picture is high fever with lobar consolidation or neutrophilia.
C. Nebulized salbutamol: for wheeze in asthma or a trial in bronchiolitis; it does not relieve pertussis paroxysms. Here there is no wheeze, just paroxysmal cough with lymphocytosis.
D. Corticosteroid: not recommended in pertussis; steroids are the answer for croup (barking cough, stridor) or asthma exacerbations, not for whooping cough.
key_concept:
Paroxysmal cough + post-tussive vomiting or cyanosis + lymphocytosis = pertussis.
  • Phases: catarrhal (URTI) then paroxysmal then convalescent
  • Lab clue: marked leukocytosis with lymphocyte predominance
  • Diagnosis: nasopharyngeal swab PCR (culture is the classic gold standard)
  • Treatment: macrolide (azithromycin preferred in young infants)
  • Same macrolide as chemoprophylaxis for close contacts
  • Common complication: pneumonia (aspiration after post-tussive vomiting)
exam_pearl: Young infants may not whoop at all; apnea or cyanosis after coughing with lymphocytosis is enough to treat as pertussis.

stem: A 4 months old child comes with right ear pain, with redness and loss of light reflex in otoscopy. Mother asks how to prevent it from occurring again?
highlight_terms_source: redness and loss of light reflex
why_right: Ear pain with a red tympanic membrane and loss of the light reflex is acute otitis media, and the mother asks about prevention of recurrence. In a 4-month-old, exclusive breastfeeding is the modifiable protective factor: it provides maternal antibodies and avoids bottle feeding in the supine position. Other preventive measures are avoiding pacifiers and tobacco smoke and keeping vaccines (pneumococcal, influenza when age-eligible) up to date.
why_wrong_block:
B. Use of pacifier: pacifier use is a recognized RISK factor for recurrent otitis media, so it should be reduced, not encouraged.
C. Daily prophylactic antibiotics: no longer recommended for recurrent otitis media because of resistance and limited benefit; frequent recurrences are referred to ENT to consider tympanostomy tubes.
key_concept:
Acute otitis media prevention focuses on modifiable risk factors.
  • Protective: breastfeeding (at least the first 6 months)
  • Avoid: pacifier use, bottle feeding while lying flat, passive smoking
  • Day care attendance increases risk
  • Vaccines: pneumococcal conjugate and annual influenza (from 6 months)
  • Recurrent AOM: ENT referral for tympanostomy tubes, not long-term antibiotics
  • Under 2 years with AOM: treat with amoxicillin
exam_pearl: If the question asks how to TREAT the current episode in an infant, the answer is amoxicillin; if it asks how to PREVENT recurrence, it is breastfeeding and risk factor removal.

stem: A 18 months old presenting with progressive pallor, SOB, fatigue and dactylitis. Labs showed Hb 70, high reticulocyte. What is the confirmatory diagnostic test?
why_right: Dactylitis (painful swelling of hands and feet) in an 18-month-old with progressive pallor, Hb 70 and high reticulocytes is the hand-foot syndrome of sickle cell disease, often its first presentation once fetal Hb falls. The smear can suggest it, but the confirmatory test for a hemoglobinopathy is hemoglobin electrophoresis, which identifies HbS.
why_wrong_block:
A. Direct Coombs test: confirms immune hemolysis (autoimmune hemolytic anemia, hemolytic disease of the newborn); it is negative in sickle cell disease and does not explain dactylitis.
C. Osmotic fragility test: the initial test for hereditary spherocytosis (spherocytes on smear, jaundice, splenomegaly, family history); it does not detect HbS.
D. LDH: a nonspecific marker of hemolysis that will be raised in many hemolytic anemias; it supports hemolysis but cannot confirm the cause.
key_concept:
Hemolytic anemia: pick the confirmatory test that matches the clue.
  • Dactylitis, painful crises: sickle cell disease, confirm with Hb electrophoresis
  • Spherocytes, family history: hereditary spherocytosis, osmotic fragility then EMA binding
  • Positive DAT: immune hemolysis
  • Bite or Heinz bodies after a trigger: G6PD deficiency, enzyme assay
  • SCD initial test: smear (sickle and target cells); confirm with electrophoresis
  • Aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19): LOW reticulocytes
exam_pearl: High reticulocytes rule out aplastic crisis; dactylitis is the giveaway pointing to sickle cell disease rather than spherocytosis.

stem: A newborn presents with microcephaly and a distended abdomen. Physical examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly. Natal history is significant for maternal diabetes. Laboratory investigations show pancytopenia and elevated AST/ALT levels. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: A newborn with microcephaly, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia and raised AST/ALT has the classic picture of a congenital (TORCH) infection, with CMV the most common cause. The next step is a congenital infection screen (TORCH serology and CMV testing in the newborn). Maternal diabetes is a distractor: it causes macrosomia, hypoglycemia and cardiac or sacral anomalies, not this picture.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chromosomal analysis: right when there are dysmorphic features or multiple structural anomalies suggesting a syndrome; it does not explain hepatitis, hepatosplenomegaly and cytopenias.
C. Abdominal ultrasound: may document organomegaly but adds nothing to the cause; the distension is already explained by hepatosplenomegaly.
D. CT abdomen: unnecessary radiation in a neonate and not diagnostic of the underlying infection.
key_concept:
Microcephaly + hepatosplenomegaly + cytopenias + hepatitis in a newborn = congenital infection until proven otherwise.
  • CMV: most common; periventricular calcification, sensorineural hearing loss
  • Toxoplasmosis: diffuse intracranial calcification, chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus
  • Rubella: cataract, PDA, deafness, microcephaly
  • Syphilis: snuffles, rash on palms and soles, bone changes
  • HSV: vesicles, encephalitis, hepatitis
exam_pearl: Maternal diabetes in the stem tempts you toward a structural workup; the combination of organ infection signs points to TORCH screening.

stem: 3 years old boy came to the clinic with poor weight gain. Over the past 4 months has loose diarrhea and intermittent abdominal pain. Physical examination and vital signs is normal. His weight on 3rd percentile and his height on 15th percentile. In the past year his weight was 36th percentile. His Abdomen is distended, non tender and normal bowel sounds. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: A 3-year-old with 4 months of loose diarrhea, intermittent abdominal pain, a distended abdomen and weight falling from the 36th to the 3rd percentile (height relatively spared) has failure to thrive from malabsorption, and celiac disease is the leading cause. The next step is serology with tissue transglutaminase IgA (checked with total IgA), done while the child is still eating gluten; positive serology then goes to duodenal biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blood gas: right for an acutely dehydrated or shocked child with suspected acidosis; this child has normal vital signs and a chronic course.
B. CBC: may show anemia but is nonspecific and will not identify the cause of chronic diarrhea and faltering weight.
D. Genetic test: HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing is mainly used to rule celiac disease OUT; it is not the first test, and other genetic tests (for example for cystic fibrosis) need a different clinical picture such as recurrent chest infections.
key_concept:
Chronic diarrhea + distension + weight dropping across percentiles after gluten introduction = test for celiac disease.
  • First test: tTG IgA plus total IgA level
  • IgA deficient: use IgG based tests
  • Confirm: endoscopy with duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy)
  • Keep gluten in the diet until testing is done
  • Treatment: lifelong gluten-free diet
  • Association: dermatitis herpetiformis, type 1 diabetes, Down syndrome
exam_pearl: Weight drops first and height follows later in malabsorption; a height that is still relatively preserved fits an evolving organic cause.

stem: Woman has long-standing right upper side pain. Imaging showed about 4 cm polypoid lesion. What is the best management?
why_right: Gallbladder polyps are managed by size, risk factors and symptoms. A 4 cm polypoid lesion is far beyond the 10 mm threshold for cholecystectomy and carries a real risk of malignancy, and the long-standing right upper pain is an additional indication on its own. Cholecystectomy (with oncological planning if malignancy is suspected on imaging) is the answer.
why_wrong_block: B. Conservative management (ultrasound surveillance) is for small asymptomatic polyps: 6 to 9 mm without risk factors, or ≤5 mm with a risk factor. A 4 cm symptomatic lesion must be removed.
key_concept:
Gallbladder polyp: decide by size, risk factors, growth and symptoms.
  • ≥10 mm: cholecystectomy
  • 6 to 9 mm + ≥1 risk factor: cholecystectomy
  • Growth ≥2 mm within 2 years: cholecystectomy
  • Unexplained gallbladder symptoms (RUQ pain): cholecystectomy
  • 6 to 9 mm without risk factors, or ≤5 mm with a risk factor: ultrasound surveillance over 2 years
exam_pearl: Symptoms alone justify cholecystectomy for a polyp, whatever its size; size ≥10 mm justifies it even without symptoms.

stem: A 35-year-old woman had abdominal ultrasound as part of screening for essential hypertension. She has no abdominal symptoms (see report). Ultrasound Abdomen: Gall bladder single polyp measures 0.6 cm, no stones, and normal bile ducts. Which is the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: This recall's key is surgical consultation for an incidental single 0.6 cm gallbladder polyp in an asymptomatic 35-year-old with no stones and normal ducts. The reasoning behind the key is that any true polyp carries some malignant potential and a surgeon should assess whether removal or surveillance is appropriate. Note that size-based guidance places this polyp in the surveillance group (see concern).
why_wrong_block:
B. A 6 to 9 mm polyp cannot simply be ignored; at minimum it needs ultrasound surveillance for growth. No follow-up is acceptable only for very small polyps without risk factors.
C. Liver function tests do not guide polyp management; the decision rests on polyp size, malignancy risk factors, growth and symptoms. The ducts are already normal on ultrasound.
D. Not the keyed answer here, although it is what size-based guidance recommends for a 6 to 9 mm polyp with no risk factors: repeat ultrasound to detect growth.
key_concept:
Gallbladder polyp management by size and risk.
  • ≥10 mm: cholecystectomy
  • 6 to 9 mm + ≥1 risk factor: cholecystectomy
  • 6 to 9 mm, no risk factors: ultrasound surveillance over 2 years
  • Growth ≥2 mm within 2 years or unexplained RUQ symptoms: cholecystectomy
  • Risk factors include older age, primary sclerosing cholangitis, Indian ethnicity, sessile polyp
exam_pearl: Exam key for this exact recall is surgical consultation; if the options make you choose by guideline size cut-offs, 6 to 9 mm without risk factors means follow-up ultrasound.

stem: A 10-month-old infant presents with irritability during feeding and recurrent vomiting. Length and head circumference are at the 25th percentile, while weight is below the 3rd percentile. The infant has two older siblings who are healthy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Weight below the 3rd percentile with length and head circumference preserved at the 25th percentile is failure to thrive. The accompanying symptoms, irritability during feeding and recurrent vomiting, point to an organic cause (for example gastroesophageal reflux disease or another gastrointestinal disorder) rather than inadequate feeding. Healthy older siblings and preserved head size argue against a genetic or chromosomal cause.
why_wrong_block:
B. Non-organic failure to thrive: right when growth faltering comes from inadequate intake or psychosocial factors (neglect, poor feeding technique) in a child WITHOUT symptoms of disease; here vomiting and feeding irritability are disease features.
C. Chromosomal abnormality: usually gives symmetric growth failure (weight, length and often head circumference all low) with dysmorphism or developmental delay, which is not described.
D. Normal variation in growth: right when a child tracks steadily along a low percentile with proportional parameters (familial short stature, constitutional delay); weight below the 3rd percentile with symptoms is never normal variation.
key_concept:
Which parameter falls first tells you the cause.
  • Weight low, length and HC preserved: inadequate intake or absorption (organic GI disease or non-organic)
  • Weight and length low, HC preserved: endocrine or constitutional causes
  • All three low, including HC: genetic, chromosomal or congenital infection
  • Symptoms (vomiting, diarrhea, feeding pain) push toward organic FTT
  • Normal child with poor intake or psychosocial concerns pushes toward non-organic FTT
exam_pearl: Do not jump to non-organic FTT just because the history is short; any disease symptom such as recurrent vomiting makes it organic.

stem: A 2-year-old child presents with cyanosis during crying and recurrent hospital admissions due to pneumonia. Bronchoscopy reveals a 90% narrowing of the lower third of the trachea during expiration. After performing a tracheostomy, what is the most appropriate next management?
highlight_terms_source: 90% narrowing of the lower third of the trachea during expiration
why_right: Cyanosis with crying, recurrent pneumonia and 90% narrowing of the lower trachea during expiration is severe tracheomalacia: the soft trachea collapses as intrathoracic pressure rises in expiration. After tracheostomy, the standard support is continuous positive airway pressure delivered through the tracheostomy, which stents the floppy airway open in expiration. This recall's key is non-invasive ventilation because it is the option that represents positive airway pressure support.
why_wrong_block:
A. Incentive spirometry: used to re-expand collapsed alveoli in post-operative atelectasis in cooperative older patients; it does not splint a collapsing trachea and a 2-year-old cannot perform it.
B. High-flow nasal cannula: gives only modest, unreliable distending pressure and is delivered through the nose, which a tracheostomy bypasses; it cannot hold a 90% collapse open.
D. Negative pressure ventilation: lowers intrathoracic pressure to draw air in and gives no positive end-expiratory pressure, so it does nothing to prevent expiratory collapse of the trachea.
key_concept:
Tracheomalacia = dynamic airway collapse; treatment = positive pressure to splint it open.
  • Clue: collapse during EXPIRATION on bronchoscopy
  • Symptoms: wheeze or stridor, barking cough, cyanotic spells with crying, recurrent pneumonia
  • Mild: most improve with growth, supportive care
  • Severe: tracheostomy plus CPAP or positive pressure ventilation via the tracheostomy
  • Alternatives in severe disease: aortopexy, tracheal stenting
exam_pearl: The same stem appears with 'Positive pressure ventilation' as an option, and then that option is the answer; the concept is always positive airway pressure.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Note: 461 is the same stem with D = Positive pressure ventilation, and there D is highlighted.

stem: A 2-year-old child presents with cyanosis during crying and recurrent hospital admissions due to pneumonia. Bronchoscopy reveals a 90% narrowing of the lower third of the trachea during expiration. After performing a tracheostomy, what is the most appropriate next management?
highlight_terms_source: 90% narrowing of the lower third of the trachea during expiration
why_right: Cyanosis with crying, recurrent pneumonia and 90% narrowing of the lower trachea during expiration is severe tracheomalacia: the soft trachea collapses as intrathoracic pressure rises in expiration. After tracheostomy, positive pressure ventilation (CPAP or ventilation with PEEP through the tracheostomy) acts as a pneumatic stent that keeps the airway open in expiration until the trachea matures.
why_wrong_block:
A. Incentive spirometry: used to re-expand collapsed alveoli in post-operative atelectasis in cooperative older patients; it does not splint a collapsing trachea and a 2-year-old cannot perform it.
B. High-flow nasal cannula: gives only modest, unreliable distending pressure through the nose, which a tracheostomy bypasses; not enough for a 90% collapse.
C. Non-invasive ventilation: delivered by mask or nasal interface, so it makes little sense once a tracheostomy is in place; it would be the choice for milder disease when avoiding a tracheostomy.
key_concept:
Tracheomalacia = dynamic airway collapse; treatment = positive pressure to splint it open.
  • Clue: collapse during EXPIRATION on bronchoscopy
  • Symptoms: wheeze or stridor, barking cough, cyanotic spells with crying, recurrent pneumonia
  • Mild: most improve with growth, supportive care
  • Severe: tracheostomy plus CPAP or positive pressure ventilation via the tracheostomy
  • Alternatives in severe disease: aortopexy, tracheal stenting
exam_pearl: Negative pressure ventilation is the trap: it gives no end-expiratory pressure, so it cannot hold a collapsing airway open.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Same stem as 460 but option D here is Positive pressure ventilation (highlighted), whereas 460 had Negative pressure ventilation and highlighted C (Non-invasive ventilation).

stem: A 2-year-old child presents with increasing difficulty in breathing and a weak cough during a family gathering. The child was previously healthy. On examination, the child is cyanotic with suprasternal and subcostal recessions. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptA: Administer oxygen and order a chest X-ray
OptD: Perform five back slaps followed by five abdominal thrusts
why_right: A previously healthy 2-year-old with sudden breathing difficulty during a family gathering (food and small objects around) is foreign body airway obstruction. A weak cough with cyanosis and recessions means the cough is ineffective (severe obstruction) in a still conscious child, so the next step is immediate relief: up to five back blows followed by up to five abdominal thrusts in a child over 1 year, repeated until the object is cleared or the child becomes unresponsive.
why_wrong_block:
A. Administer oxygen and order a chest X-ray: delays airway clearance in a cyanotic child; X-ray and bronchoscopy are for a stable child with suspected aspiration who is still moving air.
B. Give nebulized adrenaline: treats mucosal swelling in croup (barking cough, stridor after a viral prodrome); it will not move a foreign body.
C. Encourage a strong cough: right only when the cough is EFFECTIVE (loud, able to cry or speak); a weak cough with cyanosis means coughing has failed.
key_concept:
Choking algorithm depends on cough effectiveness and consciousness.
  • Effective cough: encourage coughing, observe
  • Ineffective cough, conscious, child over 1 year: back blows then abdominal thrusts
  • Ineffective cough, conscious, infant under 1 year: back blows then CHEST thrusts (no abdominal thrusts)
  • Unconscious: open airway, start CPR
  • No blind finger sweeps
exam_pearl: In an infant under 1 year the thrusts are chest thrusts, never abdominal thrusts, because of the risk of abdominal organ injury.

stem: A 3-year-old child presents with fever, shortness of breath, and cough. On examination, the respiratory rate is 50 breaths per minute. Chest examination reveals crackles in the right lower lobe. What is the most sensitive clinical finding suggestive of pneumonia in this child?
why_right: In children, tachypnea is the most sensitive clinical sign of pneumonia, and the WHO uses age-specific respiratory rate cut-offs to diagnose it in the community. A 3-year-old with RR 50 is clearly tachypneic for age. Fever, cough and shortness of breath are common in pneumonia but also occur in many other respiratory and non-respiratory illnesses.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fever: frequent but nonspecific (viral URTI, otitis, UTI) and may be absent in young infants or atypical pneumonia.
B. Shortness of breath: a subjective symptom that is hard to assess in a toddler and also occurs with asthma or bronchiolitis.
C. Cough: very common in URTI, asthma and bronchitis, so it is sensitive for respiratory illness in general but not a good discriminator for pneumonia.
key_concept:
Respiratory rate is the key bedside sign for childhood pneumonia.
  • Most sensitive sign: tachypnea for age
  • Absence of tachypnea makes pneumonia less likely
  • Severity signs: chest indrawing, grunting, hypoxia, inability to feed
  • Focal crackles support the diagnosis
  • Most common bacterial cause from 3 months to 5 years: Streptococcus pneumoniae
exam_pearl: 'Most sensitive' points to tachypnea; 'most specific' points to findings like focal crackles or consolidation on X-ray.

stem: 6 years old has bronchial asthma and complains of his acute asthma exacerbation. Which of the following is important for prevention of his exacerbation?
OptD: Patient Skills using peak flow rate
why_right: The lead-in asks what is important for prevention of exacerbations, not how to treat the current attack. Avoiding triggers (allergens such as pets, dust mites, smoke, and irritants) is the cornerstone of non-pharmacological asthma control in children and directly reduces the number of attacks. Environmental control works alongside, not instead of, a regular controller medication.
why_wrong_block:
A. Vague, nonspecific option; general education matters, but it is not a recognised specific preventive measure the way trigger avoidance is.
C. Good spacer technique improves drug delivery and is checked when asthma is uncontrolled despite treatment; it optimises therapy rather than removing the cause of attacks.
D. Peak flow monitoring helps detect worsening early and guide an action plan, and is less reliable in a 6-year-old; it monitors rather than prevents exacerbations.
key_concept:
Preventing asthma exacerbations = remove triggers + regular controller + correct technique + adherence.
  • Trigger avoidance: pets, dust mites, tobacco smoke, mould, cold air
  • Controller: daily low-dose ICS when persistent
  • Uncontrolled despite treatment: check technique and adherence before stepping up
  • Acute attack: SABA, systemic steroid, oxygen as needed
exam_pearl: 'Prevent' points to trigger control; 'uncontrolled despite inhaler' points to checking technique and adherence.

stem: An 8-year-old with poorly controlled asthma despite using an inhaler presents to the ED with a severe attack. He is not compliant with his medication and misses the inhaler 2–3 times per week. His family has two cats, and his room has good airconditioning. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: He is in the ED with a severe attack, so the next step is acute treatment, not long-term adjustment. Alongside inhaled SABA, a systemic corticosteroid (oral prednisolone in a child who can swallow) is a core part of acute exacerbation management and reduces relapse and admission. Non-compliance and the cats matter, but they are addressed once the attack is controlled.
why_wrong_block:
B. A leukotriene receptor antagonist is a later-step maintenance add-on and has no role in treating an acute severe attack.
C. Inhaled steroid is the maintenance controller he should be taking regularly; it is the answer for chronic control, not for the acute severe exacerbation in the ED.
D. Removing the cats is important for long-term prevention, but it does nothing for the severe attack happening now.
key_concept:
Acute vs chronic: in the ED treat the attack first, then fix the cause.
  • Acute: SABA (plus ipratropium if severe), systemic steroid, oxygen, IV magnesium if poor response
  • After stabilisation: adherence, inhaler technique, trigger control
  • Chronic control: daily ICS, step up per ladder
exam_pearl: 'Presents to ED with severe attack' + 'next step' = acute therapy (systemic steroid), even when the stem lists triggers and non-compliance.

stem: A 10-year-old child presents with severe asthma exacerbation. He uses an inhaler twice daily (unspecified), has two cats at home, and has poor compliance with his medications. His room is well-ventilated. Asking what is the most important factor in managing this patient?
why_right: The stem stresses two cats at home and poor compliance, and asks for the most important factor in managing this child overall. Exposure to a persistent allergen trigger keeps provoking exacerbations whatever medication is added, so removing it is the key modifiable factor. This recall's key is environmental control, since adding or changing drugs will not help while the trigger persists and adherence is poor.
why_wrong_block:
A. Low-dose corticosteroid is a controller step; he is probably already on a twice-daily inhaler, and drug changes fail while the trigger and non-adherence persist.
B. A leukotriene receptor antagonist is a step-up add-on, used only after adherence, technique and triggers have been addressed.
C. Inhaled steroid is the standard controller, but he likely already has one; adding it does not address the cats, which drive his attacks.
key_concept:
Before stepping up asthma therapy, check the simple things first.
  • Adherence and inhaler technique
  • Trigger exposure: pets, smoke, dust mites
  • Comorbidities: rhinitis, reflux
  • Only then step up the controller
exam_pearl: Stem names a pet or other trigger and asks for the 'most important factor' = environmental control, not another drug.

stem: 11 years girl came to evaluation of fatigue for the last month, she has history of joint pain in knees and hands, malar rash and photosensitivity. After that came to ER complaining of headache, confusion and generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Initiated on iv methylprednisolone and positive for anti-dsDna. Labs: Normal creatinine, Normal urine, Decreased C3 and C4, Negative ANA. Which of the following drug should be added:
why_right: Malar rash, photosensitivity, arthritis, positive anti-dsDNA and low C3/C4 indicate SLE, and the new headache, confusion and generalized seizure mean neuropsychiatric lupus. Severe organ-threatening lupus needs high-dose steroid pulses plus an induction immunosuppressant, and for CNS lupus that agent is cyclophosphamide. Normal creatinine and urine show no nephritis, which would otherwise favour mycophenolate.
why_wrong_block:
A. Rituximab is a second-line or refractory option in severe lupus, not the standard first agent added for neuropsychiatric SLE.
C. Hydroxychloroquine is background therapy for almost all SLE patients and alone suits mild skin and joint disease; it is not enough for active CNS lupus.
D. Mycophenolate is the preferred induction agent for lupus nephritis; here creatinine and urine are normal, and the threatened organ is the brain.
key_concept:
Match the SLE add-on drug to the organ involved.
  • Skin and joints (mild): hydroxychloroquine with or without methotrexate
  • Kidney (nephritis): mycophenolate
  • CNS (seizures, psychosis, confusion): IV steroid pulse + cyclophosphamide
  • Refractory disease: rituximab
  • Anti-dsDNA and low C3/C4 track disease activity
exam_pearl: Seizure or psychosis in lupus = cyclophosphamide; nephritis = mycophenolate.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Better recall of 467. Original: 'Patient have SLE symptoms (did not mention diagnosis directly) with seizures and confusion (CNS symptoms) received methylprednisone, what additional drug should she receive?' Options Azathioprine / Hydroxychloroquine / Cyclophosphamide (highlighted) / Methotrexate.

stem: Patient came to outpatient clinic today he mentioned he had an RTA 1 week ago and complaining of mild abdominal pain after accident. O/E: Vitally stable. Mild abdominal pain mainly in the right upper quadrant. No other complaints or findings. What is the most appropriate next step?
OptB: Refer him to emergency department for further evaluation
OptC: Do blood work to rule out hemorrhage
why_right: A vitally stable outpatient with only mild RUQ pain one week after an RTA and no other findings needs a non-invasive look for a delayed or missed solid organ injury (liver laceration, subcapsular hematoma, contained collection). Abdominal ultrasound is quick, radiation-free, available in clinic and appropriate as the next step in a stable patient; abnormal findings or deterioration then lead to CT and admission.
why_wrong_block:
B. ED referral is right if the patient is unstable, has peritonitis, worsening pain or abnormal findings; this patient is stable with mild pain, so an immediate ED transfer is not the most appropriate first step.
C. Blood tests (Hb, LFT) may support but cannot localize or exclude an organ injury; a normal Hb a week later does not rule out a hematoma, so imaging is the decisive step.
key_concept:
Abdominal pain after blunt trauma: hemodynamic status decides the pathway.
  • Unstable + free fluid on FAST: laparotomy
  • Stable: CT abdomen with contrast is the definitive test in the acute setting
  • Stable outpatient with mild late pain: ultrasound first, escalate to CT if abnormal
  • Delayed splenic/hepatic rupture can present days after trauma
exam_pearl: Stability is the switch: stable patient gets imaging, unstable patient gets the operating room or emergency department.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q (other version): vitals were given as numbers in a large table, all within normal range; same options, A highlighted.

stem: 45-year-old patient who was incidentally found on ultrasound (US) to have an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) measuring 4.5 cm. What to do?
why_right: An incidental, asymptomatic 4.5 cm AAA is below the elective repair threshold (5.5 cm in men, 5 cm in women). Below that size the risk of rupture is lower than the risk of operating, so the aneurysm is followed with serial ultrasound, together with risk factor control (smoking cessation, BP and lipid control).
why_wrong_block: A. Immediate surgery is for a ruptured or symptomatic (tender, painful) aneurysm; elective repair is for diameter above the threshold or rapid growth. A 4.5 cm asymptomatic AAA meets none of these.
key_concept:
AAA: size, symptoms and growth decide.
  • Initial imaging and surveillance: ultrasound
  • Confirm/plan (stable, symptomatic or before repair or other abdominal surgery): CT angiography
  • Asymptomatic, below threshold: surveillance + risk factor control
  • Repair: ≥5.5 cm men, ≥5 cm women, growth >1 cm/year, symptomatic or ruptured
exam_pearl: Any pain, tenderness or rupture overrides size: a symptomatic AAA of any diameter goes for repair.

stem: 70 years old known HTN and smoker on routine check up found Aortic Aneurism 4.5 cm. What is the management?
why_right: A 4.5 cm aneurysm found on routine check-up (asymptomatic) in a 70-year-old is below the repair threshold (5.5 cm in men, 5 cm in women), so the answer is ultrasound surveillance with risk factor control, here stopping smoking and controlling his hypertension. Surveillance intervals vary between guidelines; the principle is regular imaging to detect growth.
why_wrong_block:
B. EVAR is a method of repair, used once repair is indicated (≥5.5 cm, growth >1 cm/year, symptoms or rupture) and anatomy is suitable; not indicated at 4.5 cm.
C. Open surgical repair has the same indications as EVAR (often chosen in younger, fit patients or unsuitable anatomy); below threshold its operative risk outweighs rupture risk.
key_concept:
AAA below threshold = watch; above threshold, symptomatic or fast-growing = repair (EVAR or open).
  • Repair threshold: ≥5.5 cm men, ≥5 cm women
  • Rapid growth >1 cm/year: repair
  • Symptomatic or ruptured: repair regardless of size
  • Below threshold: ultrasound surveillance, stop smoking, BP and lipid control
exam_pearl: Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for AAA growth; stopping it is part of the answer when you choose surveillance.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q: variant shown under 469.

stem: A Male patient has carotid artery stenosis 48% high-risk, old age, multiple comorbidities dyslipidemia and HTN, slurred speech. What is the next step in management for this patient?
why_right: With 48% stenosis, even with symptoms (slurred speech), the degree of narrowing is below the 50% level at which revascularization offers benefit, and this patient is high-risk, elderly with multiple comorbidities, making procedural risk outweigh any gain. The keyed 'observation' means no intervention on the artery: best medical therapy (antiplatelet, high-intensity statin, BP control) with follow-up imaging.
why_wrong_block:
B. Carotid stenting is an alternative to endarterectomy for significant symptomatic stenosis (≥50%, mainly 70 to 99%) in patients at high surgical risk; at 48% there is no indication for revascularization.
C. Endarterectomy benefits symptomatic patients with 70 to 99% stenosis (and selected 50 to 69%), ideally soon after the event; below 50% it gives no benefit and adds operative stroke risk.
key_concept:
Symptomatic carotid stenosis: degree of stenosis decides.
  • 70 to 99%: carotid endarterectomy, early after the event
  • 50 to 69%: consider endarterectomy in selected patients
  • <50%: best medical therapy only
  • Stenting: alternative when surgical risk is high and stenosis is significant
  • Near-total occlusion/complete occlusion: no surgery
exam_pearl: 'Observation' in carotid questions still means antiplatelet + statin + risk factor control, never doing nothing after a neurological symptom.

stem: 21-year-women presented to Emergency Room with right lower quadrant pain and anorexia. RLQ tenderness and rebound tenderness, WBC high. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: right lower quadrant pain and anorexia
why_right: The picture (RLQ pain, anorexia, rebound tenderness, high WBC) suggests appendicitis, but this is a 21-year-old woman, in whom gynecological causes (ovarian torsion, ruptured cyst, ectopic pregnancy, PID) commonly mimic it. The key chooses CT abdomen, the most sensitive test, to confirm the diagnosis and exclude complications or alternatives before operating. A pregnancy test should precede any CT in a woman of reproductive age.
why_wrong_block:
A. Proceeding straight to surgery is reasonable only when the diagnosis is clear (e.g. a young man with classic findings), and the preferred approach today is laparoscopic, not open; in a young woman the diagnosis should be confirmed first.
C. Peritoneal signs (rebound tenderness) with leukocytosis can never be discharged; discharge fits only when examination and labs are reassuring.
key_concept:
Suspected appendicitis: choose imaging by patient group.
  • Adults, obese patients: CT abdomen (best sensitivity)
  • Children and pregnant women: ultrasound first, MRI if equivocal in pregnancy
  • Woman of reproductive age: β-hCG first, gynecological causes in the differential
  • Clear clinical diagnosis: appendectomy (laparoscopic preferred)
  • Abscess: drainage + antibiotics; phlegmon: antibiotics, conservative
exam_pearl: Young woman with RLQ pain: confirm before cutting; if she is pregnant, the imaging switches from CT to ultrasound/MRI.

stem: An 8-year-old girl presented to the Emergency Room with severe abdominal pain for the last 6 hours. The pain is constant and not relieved by acetaminophen. She cannot stand up straight because of the pain. Physical Examination reveals a mild grade fever with severe abdominal tenderness over the right lower quadrant and rebound tenderness. Which of the following imaging study is the most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: right lower quadrant and rebound tenderness
why_right: Six hours of constant pain, low-grade fever, and right lower quadrant and rebound tenderness in an 8-year-old are acute appendicitis. This recall's key is CT abdomen because the lead-in says confirm, and CT has the highest sensitivity and specificity for appendicitis. In children, however, ultrasound is the first-line imaging to avoid radiation, and CT is kept for equivocal ultrasound or suspected complications.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ultrasound is the first-line imaging in children and pregnancy and is favoured by many; this key picks CT as the most accurate confirmatory test.
C. MRI avoids radiation and is used mainly in pregnancy when ultrasound is inconclusive; it is not the routine confirmatory test here.
D. MRCP images the biliary and pancreatic ducts and has no role in right lower quadrant pain.
key_concept:
Appendicitis imaging depends on the patient and the lead-in verb.
  • Non-pregnant adult: CT is best
  • Child or pregnant woman: ultrasound first
  • Equivocal ultrasound in pregnancy: MRI
  • Suspected abscess or phlegmon: CT at any age
exam_pearl: 'Initial/first line' in a child suggests ultrasound; 'most accurate/confirm' suggests CT.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q: variant shown under 471.

stem: pregnant lady with RLQ pain vomiting, tenderness and leukocytosis, appropriate treatment
OptA: CT Abdomen and US (In one option)
key_concept:
Appendicitis in pregnancy: confirm with radiation-sparing imaging, then antibiotics plus appendectomy.
  • Imaging: US first in pregnant women and children; MRI if US inconclusive
  • CT: best sensitivity in non-pregnant adults; any age for abscess or phlegmon
  • Uncomplicated: empirical antibiotics + laparoscopic appendectomy
  • Phlegmon: IV antibiotics (conservative)
  • Abscess: percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics + interval appendectomy
exam_pearl: Read the verb: "confirm/diagnose" points to imaging (US first in pregnancy), "treatment" points to antibiotics with appendectomy, never discharge.

Compiler note: Q: variant shown under 471; no answer marked.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: old patient underwent laparotomy 4 days ago and post-operatively developed absent bowel sounds, abdominal distension and can't pass stool, no fever or high Wbc. What is the most appropriate initial management?
why_right: Laparotomy "4 days ago" followed by "absent bowel sounds", distension and failure to pass stool, with "no fever or high WBC", is postoperative paralytic ileus. Ileus is managed conservatively, and the initial step is bowel rest with nasogastric decompression and IV fluids (with electrolyte correction). Most cases settle without intervention.
why_wrong_block:
A. Laxatives add load to a bowel that is not moving and are not used in ileus; early ambulation helps but is supportive only. Laxatives fit simple constipation with a working bowel.
C. Laparotomy is for peritonitis, strangulation or failure of conservative management; here there is no fever, no leukocytosis and no peritoneal signs.
key_concept:
Early postoperative ileus = conservative care first.
  • Surgery days ago: paralytic ileus or Ogilvie; surgery years ago: adhesive obstruction
  • Ileus: dilated small and large bowel, no transition point
  • Conservative: NPO, NGT decompression, IV fluids, correct electrolytes
  • Prolonged ileus: check potassium (hypokalemia causes ileus)
  • Operate only for peritonitis, strangulation or failed conservative care
exam_pearl: If "check serum potassium/electrolytes" is offered as the next step for prolonged ileus, that is the keyed choice in similar questions.

stem: A Hypertensive man On Aspirin came with a bright red spot in his eye, he denied pain, visual changes, no signs of infection, what's the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: bright red spot in his eye
why_right: A hypertensive man on aspirin with a bright red spot, no pain, no visual change and no infection signs has a subconjunctival hemorrhage. Both hypertension and antiplatelet therapy predispose to rupture of small conjunctival vessels; the condition is benign and resolves without treatment.
why_wrong_block:
A. Conjunctivitis gives diffuse injection with discharge and irritation; there are no infection signs and the redness is a localised patch.
B. Scleritis is severely painful and tender with a deep violet hue, often linked to autoimmune disease; this eye is painless.
C. Episcleritis shows sectoral engorged vessels with mild discomfort, not a flat sheet of extravasated blood.
key_concept:
Painless bright red patch, normal vision, no discharge = subconjunctival hemorrhage.
  • Risks: hypertension, aspirin or anticoagulants, Valsalva, trauma
  • Management: reassure, check BP; no need to stop aspirin for this alone
  • On warfarin or recurrent: check INR or bleeding screen
exam_pearl: Add pain, photophobia or reduced vision and it is no longer a subconjunctival hemorrhage question.

stem: 60 Y/O female, had large amount of Maroon-colored stool, she is pale and tachycardic, continued to bleed despite good resuscitation, abdomen is lax and soft and non tender, what is the initial management?
highlight_terms_source: continued to bleed despite good resuscitation
why_right: This recall's key is NGT because the lead-in asks for the initial management of "large amount of maroon-colored stool" with tachycardia and ongoing bleeding. Brisk upper GI bleeding can present as maroon or bright red stool, so the classic first step is to exclude an upper source with nasogastric aspiration before committing to a lower GI work-up. A bilious aspirate without blood makes an upper source less likely.
why_wrong_block:
B. Angiography localizes and embolizes active bleeding in a patient still bleeding despite resuscitation; it is the definitive next step after an upper source is excluded, which the twin recall keys for "most appropriate" management.
C. Colonoscopy suits a stable patient who can tolerate bowel preparation; massive ongoing bleeding in an unstable patient limits views and safety.
D. Barium enema has no role in acute bleeding: it cannot treat, rarely localizes active bleeding and obscures later angiography or endoscopy.
key_concept:
Massive hematochezia: resuscitate, exclude an upper source, then localize and treat.
  • Maroon or red stool + instability: think brisk upper GI bleed too
  • Exclude upper source: NG aspirate (classic) or upper endoscopy
  • Unstable or ongoing bleeding: CT angiography, then catheter angiography with embolization
  • Stable, tolerating prep: colonoscopy
  • No source: tagged RBC scan and small bowel evaluation
exam_pearl: Same scenario, two keys: "initial" = NGT (rule out upper source), "most appropriate" = angiography.

stem: 60 Y/O female, had large amount of Maroon-colored stool, she is pale and tachycardic, continued to bleed despite good resuscitation, abdomen is lax and soft and non tender, what is the Most Appropriate Management?
highlight_terms_source: continued to bleed despite good resuscitation
why_right: A 60-year-old with "large amount of maroon-colored stool", pale and tachycardic, who "continued to bleed despite good resuscitation" has ongoing hemodynamically significant lower GI bleeding. For the most appropriate management, angiography (CT angiography, then catheter angiography) localizes the active bleeding point and allows embolization without bowel preparation. The soft, non-tender abdomen argues against ischemia or peritonitis needing surgery.
why_wrong_block:
A. NGT aspiration is the classic initial step to exclude an upper source of maroon stool (keyed in the twin "initial" recall), but it does not stop or localize lower GI bleeding.
C. Colonoscopy is first for a stable patient able to tolerate bowel preparation; with ongoing massive bleeding and instability, angiography is preferred.
D. Barium enema is never used in acute bleeding: it neither treats nor reliably localizes bleeding and interferes with later angiography or endoscopy.
key_concept:
Acute LGIB: stability decides the route.
  • Unstable: stabilize (large-bore IV, blood products, reverse anticoagulation) then CT angiography
  • Stable + can take prep + low suspicion of active bleeding: colonoscopy
  • Source found: hemostasis (endoscopic or embolization)
  • No source: colonoscopy if not done, then tagged RBC scan and small bowel evaluation
  • Surgery: failure of these or peritonitis
exam_pearl: "Initial" in the twin recall flips the key to NGT; "most appropriate" with ongoing bleeding means angiography.

stem: Old women presented with lower gi bleeding; on examination diffusely tender abdomen, pr exam showing fresh blood, patient is unstable despite receiving blood (BP Was Not Mentioned, Just Unstable). What is the most appropriate Next Step In Management:
key_concept:
LGIB next step depends on stability and peritoneal signs.
  • Unstable: resuscitate, then CT angiography and embolization
  • Stable + tolerates prep: colonoscopy
  • Peritonitis, ischemia or failed angiography: laparotomy
  • Coagulopathy: correct (FFP, reversal) alongside, not instead of, source control
  • No source found: tagged RBC scan, small bowel evaluation
exam_pearl: A soft non-tender abdomen with ongoing bleeding pushes to angiography; a diffusely tender abdomen raises ischemia or peritonitis and pushes toward surgery.

stem: child was diagnosed with acute glomerulonephritis, and the parents are asking, When does the C3 level return to normal?
why_right: In acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis C3 is consumed and falls transiently, then recovers as the immune-complex process settles. This recall's key is 3 to 4 weeks, the closest listed option to the expected recovery period, since the other choices are clearly too short or far too long. Standard teaching gives normalisation within about 6 to 8 weeks, and persistence beyond that should prompt a search for another diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Too early; C3 is still typically low 1 to 2 weeks into the illness.
C. Far too long for PSGN; C3 still low after about 8 to 12 weeks suggests membranoproliferative or C3 glomerulopathy, or lupus nephritis, and warrants biopsy.
key_concept:
PSGN complement: low C3 and normal C4, with recovery in weeks.
  • Onset 1 to 3 weeks after pharyngitis, longer after impetigo
  • C3 typically normalises within 6 to 8 weeks
  • Persistently low C3: think MPGN, C3 glomerulopathy or lupus nephritis
  • Treatment is supportive: salt and fluid restriction, antihypertensives
exam_pearl: Low C3 lasting beyond 8 weeks means it is not simple PSGN.

stem: A 6-year-old boy has a severe respiratory infection and has not received any vaccines due to family concern. Which vaccine would you recommend to decrease such complications in the future?
why_right: The child had a severe respiratory infection and is fully unvaccinated, and the vaccine asked for should cut future serious respiratory complications. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the leading bacterial cause of severe pneumonia, bacteremia and empyema in children, so this recall's key is PCV. It directly targets the organism behind complicated respiratory infection.
why_wrong_block:
A. DTaP prevents diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis; it is part of his catch-up, but pneumococcus is the main cause of complicated pneumonia.
B. OPV prevents poliomyelitis, a neurological disease, and does nothing to reduce respiratory infection complications.
key_concept:
Match the vaccine to the disease it prevents.
  • PCV: pneumococcal pneumonia, bacteremia, meningitis, otitis
  • Hib: epiglottitis, meningitis
  • DTaP: pertussis, diphtheria, tetanus
  • OPV/IPV: polio
  • Unvaccinated child: catch up, never restart a series
exam_pearl: 'Prevent severe respiratory complications' = PCV; 'prevent whooping cough' = DTaP.

stem: 6 years child with panhypopituitarism. He is on multiple hormonal treatments. Initial evaluation revealed short stature and delayed bone age. Other hormonal studies are normal.

  • Cortisol: hydrocortisone (replace first)
  • Thyroid: levothyroxine
  • GH: recombinant GH when deficiency is confirmed (low IGF-1, failed stimulation tests)
  • Sex steroids: at pubertal age
  • Growth velocity over about 6 months helps when the GH status is unclear

stem: 5 years old child found to have an abdominal mass and on his examination he had reduced air entry on multiple sites. What's the most important test to assess his condition or the disease?
highlight_terms_source: reduced air entry on multiple sites
why_right: An abdominal mass in a 5-year-old suggests a childhood solid tumour, most often Wilms tumour or neuroblastoma, and the reduced air entry hints at lung spread. This recall's key is abdominal ultrasound, the first and most useful test to define the mass: organ of origin, solid vs cystic, and renal vein or IVC involvement. It is radiation-free and guides all further imaging.
why_wrong_block:
A. Nuclear studies (bone scan or MIBG) are used for staging, mainly in neuroblastoma, after the mass has been characterised.
B. Chest CT stages lung metastases and is part of the workup once a tumour is found, but it does not characterise the abdominal mass.
D. Plain abdominal X-ray may show calcification or mass effect but cannot define organ of origin or extent.
key_concept:
Paediatric abdominal mass workup.
  • First: abdominal ultrasound (origin, solid or cystic, vascular invasion)
  • Then: CT or MRI abdomen for detail
  • Staging: chest CT for lung metastases (Wilms commonly spreads to the lung)
  • Neuroblastoma: urine catecholamines, MIBG scan
exam_pearl: Characterise the mass with ultrasound first; chest CT is for staging the lungs.

stem: Female pt came with epigastric pain with nausea and vomiting. O/E tenderness of the epigastric region. (It was very short Q no other predisposing factors or S&S) Amylase was high No other labs were mentioned. What will predict the severity of her case (something like that)
why_right: Epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting with epigastric tenderness and "amylase was high" is acute pancreatitis. The question asks what will predict severity: CRP is the standard single biochemical marker of severity, with a markedly raised level at about 48 hours indicating severe disease. It is cheap, widely available and reliable once enough time has passed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Procalcitonin rises earlier and is used to suggest infected necrosis or as an early marker within the first day; for a general severity question without timing, CRP is the keyed marker.
B. A raised ALT points to a gallstone (biliary) cause of pancreatitis; it identifies the etiology, not the severity.
D. ESR is a slow, nonspecific inflammatory marker with no role in grading acute pancreatitis.
key_concept:
Pancreatitis: diagnose with 2 of 3, grade severity separately.
  • Diagnosis: typical pain, amylase/lipase ≥3× ULN, typical imaging
  • Severity marker: CRP (best at about 48 hours)
  • Scores: Ranson, Glasgow, APACHE II, BISAP
  • Raised ALT: suggests biliary cause
  • Procalcitonin: early marker, infected necrosis
exam_pearl: If the stem gives a short duration (hours, under a day), the related recall keys procalcitonin because CRP has not yet risen.
